contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
contributions.text_english: Diolch yn fawr, Lywydd. Before I start, I just want to say, it's been a sad day today. I stood in Aberfan this morning. I stood side by side with that community, which came together in unity in the face of such adversity. But it's been a terrible, shameful, shameless end to a sad day. A sad day indeed when those benches bring into this Siambr—those who are here to represent the whole of Wales, all our communities, all our citizens—that which seeks to divide those communities. I've listened carefully to the contributions this evening. I've been disturbed by such an unsettling sound, because, Llywydd, you don't have to strain hard at all, do you, anymore, to hear the dog whistle that has too often pierced political debates in this Chamber since the election in May? [Interruption.] Yes, Vikki.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
contributions.text_english:
Absolutely, and properly represent their communities and the voice of their communities. Absolutely. That dog whistle varies in volume, it's always there, but it's getting louder. It lingers over those benches, a deliberately intangible thing that leaves too many wondering whether a line has been crossed. Llywydd, I am not afraid to speak up and say that, since May, that line has too often been crossed. It hides itself in plain sight: hateful speech dressed up as free speech over concerns—[Interruption.] No, we've heard enough from those benches, thank you very much. It lurks beneath what is disingenuously tonight presented as the language of common sense and—I'm not taking interventions—in today's case, British values. [Interruption.] Llywydd, can I carry on?

I want the Members who have spoken in support of this debate to know that not only do we hear you but we see you. We see you for what you are. We see you weaponising discontent, driving division and stirring hate. We see you in this debate conflating the intimidating behaviour of thugs—those whose protests can descend into disorder and violence, often in demonstrations directed against migrants or Muslims—with the very people who are targeted by that intimidating behaviour.

Llywydd, let me say clearly that I do not accept the premise that face coverings are in themselves contrary to our values. Such a catch-all position ignores the many legitimate reasons why face coverings are worn. People's rights to do so can, of course, be subject already to lawful and proportionate restrictions when necessary, including to prevent crime and disorder. But the justification comes from the situation and the behaviour, not from a judgment that covering one's face in itself is unacceptable and dangerous.

contributions.text_english: Yes.
contributions.text_original: Yes.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
contributions.text_english:
Absolutely. And the people of Neath showed—. We had a food fair recently where they were there out in the street. They had never had so much support and so many donations after those. The people of Neath came out and they spoke in support of the fine men and women of the RNLI.

One of the reasons for wearing a face covering is, of course, an important one that I am determined to use my voice to defend: religious expression. The values of our nation are centred not on exclusion but on respect, and we as representatives of our communities should respect people of every religion within them and we should never suggest that they are in any way less or inferior because they exercise their human right to freedom of religion. People of every religion or belief should feel that they belong in Wales. I do not accept that a face covering worn by an individual for religious reasons means they don't share British or Welsh values. Nor should we suggest that someone belongs any less because their religious practice differs from that of others.

Framing religious dress as contrary to British values without demonstrating any harm that justifies interference with fundamental rights risks deepening division rather than strengthening cohesion. But this is clearly Reform UK's aim here. The Jewish people of 1930s Germany were subject to the Nuremberg laws that stated they were no longer German, laws that led to their persecution and extermination by the state that stripped them of their German-ness, enabled by those who believed German-ness could not accommodate diversity. Who is the arbiter of Britishness or Welshness? Who decides that a woman who wears a face covering is less British or less Welsh? We have a moral duty and responsibility in this place to be careful about the language we use and the message we send and not to engage or encourage discrimination on the basis of race, religion or belief.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
contributions.text_english:
Thank you. It was a statement of fact about what happened in Germany in the 1930s. The face coverings debate, when it is spoken about by Reform UK, is always referencing connection with religious dress. On 6 October, the deputy leader set out their position in this Chamber: they would ban the burqa and every full-face covering in public. The debate put forward on this subject in the Scottish Parliament also specifically references the burqa and niqab as the only face coverings mentioned. This dog-whistle politics, while almost always a disturbing undercurrent where Reform UK is concerned, pierces the surface of this debate and other debates more and more often.

But then there are occasions where the racism, sexism and misogyny of Reform UK is plain to see. ITV's exposure Undercover: A Year in Reform, broadcast just a few days ago, recorded Reform UK members and representatives describing Asian families as parasites. A Reform candidate in Wales who was employed by the Member that brought this debate to the Chamber was recorded using abhorrent racist terms. Unsurprisingly, it also exposed the misogyny and sexism within the party—so much for a party who so often claims to want to protect women and girls. And we, as women of all races and religions, stand as one against this behaviour, this language and the so-called values of your party.

contributions.text_english: No-one should tell a woman what to wear. Respect for women means respect for every woman—respecting the fact that every woman can make her own choices. Home Office figures published last week showed a 13 per cent increase in religious hate crimes recorded by the police during the year up to March of this year. With a total of 11,419 recorded offences, there was a 15 per cent increase in hate crimes targeting Muslims. Respondents shared experiences of being physically attacked, threatened, spat upon and having their religious attire mocked and targeted.

Roedd ffigurau'r Swyddfa Gartref a gyhoeddwyd yr wythnos diwethaf yn dangos cynnydd o 13 y cant mewn troseddau casineb crefyddol a gofnodwyd gan yr heddlu yn ystod y flwyddyn hyd at Fawrth eleni. Gyda chyfanswm o 11,419 o droseddau wedi eu cofnodi, o'r rheini roedd cynnydd o 15 y cant mewn troseddau casineb sy'n targedu Mwslimiaid. Rhannodd ymatebwyr brofiadau o gael eu hymosod yn gorfforol, eu bygwth, cael pobl yn poeri arnynt a gweld eu gwisg crefyddol yn cael ei gwawdio a'i thargedu.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
contributions.text_english: These crimes aren't just happening in faraway towns and cities, as we heard from Kiera Marshall, they're happening in our communities. When I visited a mosque in September, members of the Muslim community told me about the profound impact that Islamaphobia is having on them and how that attack, in which a Welsh Muslim woman had had her hijab torn from her head, was affecting their sense of safety and belonging.

When I visited a mosque in September, members of the Muslim community told me about the profound impact that Islamaphobia is having on them and how that attack, in which a Welsh Muslim woman had had her hijab torn from her head, was affecting their sense of safety and belonging.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
contributions.text_english:
I absolutely agree that it's shameful. And what's also shameful is the claim that Muslim women are somehow voiceless and forced to dress against their will. That's as sexist as it is Islamaphobic. These experiences and the stubbornly high rates of hate crime don't happen by accident, they happen by design. They do so by deliberately pitting communities against each other for political gain, which is as shameful as it is hateful.

The philosopher Hannah Arendt, herself deemed 'un-German' and forced to flee her native land, warned that the death of human empathy is one of the earliest and most telling signs of a culture on the verge of descending into barbarism. What can stop that descent is the power and protection of universal human rights. So, if we are to talk about British values, let us talk first and foremost about those rights, those freedoms that are enshrined in British laws: the freedom of religion—everyone in Wales is protected by the Equality Act 2010 and the Human Rights Act 1998—a freedom that Reform appear to have a problem with. Because the pattern is always the same: they claim to be champions of freedom—[Interruption.]—no, I won't—but only when it fits their narrow and singular definition, a dangerous, exclusionary definition. We must never be bystanders to bigotry and hatred.

And, Llywydd, this Government will always celebrate the plurality of our communities. We will always challenge those who claim that our differences divide us. Our values are demonstrated by how we treat one another. In her report on the war crimes trial of the Nazi Adolf Eichmann, Hannah Arendt suggested that his evil stemmed from an inability to think from the standpoint of someone else. That lack of empathy, that ability to see others as less, is what we must constantly guard against in this society. And that empathy must be expressed by those with power and influence through the language they use.

So, finally, Llywydd, at a time when racism and Islamaphobia, fuelled by deliberate political discourse, are becoming increasingly normalised, we should remind ourselves that we, as elected Members in this Chamber, hold a position of privilege and of power. contributions.item_title_en: 7. The Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Revocation and Transitional Provision) (Wales) (Amendment) Order 2026
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd, and I move the motion to approve the Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Revocation and Transitional Provision) (Wales) (Amendment) Order 2026. This is a short and technical amending instrument that is required to keep the statute book clear, accurate and consistent. The Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Revocation and Transitional Provision) (Wales) (Amendment) Order 2026 will replace the Child Minding and Day Care Exceptions (Wales) Order 2010 from 1 April 2027.

As a consequence of the revoking and replacing of the 2010 exceptions Order with the 2026 exceptions Order, references to the 2010 exceptions Order in existing legislation must be updated. This amendment Order makes these necessary changes. This amendment Order replaces relevant references to the 2010 exceptions Order on the statute book with references to the 2026 exceptions Order.

This amendment Order does not alter the policies set out in the 2026 exceptions Order. It creates no new duties, makes no changes to existing processes, and imposes no new requirements on providers, families or public bodies.

The proposals for the 2026 exceptions Order were consulted upon in 2025. I'm content that no further consultation was required for this consequential amendment instrument because its changes are minor and of a technical nature. This amendment Order only updates legislative cross-references to ensure that the statute book is accurate.

I am aware that further consequential amendments are required to legislation within the competence of the United Kingdom and Scottish Governments. These are minor and technical amendments to update references to the 2010 exceptions Order to ensure consistency and accuracy. My officials are working with both Governments to support these amendments to be made prior to the 2026 exceptions Order coming into force. I therefore ask Members to approve this necessary technical Order. Thank you.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Legislative Consent Motion: The Armed Forces Bill
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. I move the motion, and I recommend that the Senedd does consent to the relevant provisions in the Armed Forces Bill 2026, as is outlined in the legislative consent motion laid for this Bill.  

The Bill introduces provisions across a broad range of areas related to the armed forces, in devolved and reserved areas alike. These include: renewing the Armed Forces Act 2006; expanding the legal duty to give due regard to the armed forces covenant to include the UK Government and the devolved Governments; to create a new defence housing service to improve standards in defence housing and their supply; improving the measures that safeguard against sexual and violent conduct, stalking and harassment; and modernising support for victims of crimes committed by the armed forces.

We believe that a number of the Bill's provisions relate to devolved services, and our legislative consent memorandum reflects this. The UK Government agrees with us that clause 2 of the armed forces covenant initiates the legislative consent memorandum process. We are also of the view that clauses related to the new defence housing service, the support of victims in the justice system with regard to the armed forces, the management of criminals, and the Reserve Forces' and Cadets' Associations may impact devolved areas. 

Members will be familiar with the armed forces covenant: the pledge that we will together, as a nation, recognise and understand that those who serve or who have served in the armed forces, and their families, including those who have faced bereavement, should be treated fairly and should not face disadvantage. Extending the legal duties of the armed forces covenant through this Bill is something that we therefore welcome as a Government, and it aligns with the commitment made in our programme for government.

Our support for services like the Veterans' NHS Wales, armed forces liaison officers, and Supporting Service Children in Education in Wales are examples of the ways that we ensure that the covenant is visible to the armed forces community. We offer practical steps, not just warm words. This duty will hold us to account, alongside other public bodies, and we welcome this.

The covenant element of the Bill will also expand the current duty to 11 additional policy areas, including childcare, social care, personal taxation and transport. This is a significant expansion of the duty's scope. I have emphasised to the UK Government that the resources, the training and the guidance must be available to all bodies subject to the duty so that it is truly embedded and to ensure that it makes a real difference to the armed forces community.

Dirprwy Lywydd, the Armed Forces Bill 2026 provides a suitable platform for ensuring that the services and policies consider the armed forces community's circumstances appropriately the length and breadth of the UK. By the same token, it offers a way to improve housing for armed forces families and improves safeguarding measures for the victims of crimes committed by the armed forces. It also provides greater safeguards against sexual and violent conduct, stalking and harassment for members of the armed forces, including those based here in Wales.

I'm grateful to the Legislation Committee and the Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee, and I thank Members for their scrutiny of the Bill. I note that both committees agree with our assessment of the Bill's provisions that call for the Senedd's consent. I'm also aware that the Legislation Committee has noted that the deadline of a fortnight for laying the legislative consent memorandum was not met, and that I had not initially confirmed a recommendation for consent to be granted. We recognise the difficulties that delays in laying legislative consent memoranda can cause in terms of committee scrutiny. I also recognise the importance of laying legislative consent memoranda as soon as possible, rather than delaying them until the Welsh Government has come to a final conclusion in terms of its recommendations. I recognise the importance of providing clear recommendations for the Senedd on legislative consent memoranda as soon as possible to support effective scrutiny. I was able to inform the committees of our stance only when correspondence with the UK Government had been completed.

In terms of the changes to the scope of the covenant's duties and guidance, Members will be aware that I wrote to the UK Government in July requesting a requirement for the Welsh Ministers to give their consent, thereby ensuring stronger constitutional safeguards for the role of Welsh Ministers in relation to the covenant. I'm pleased that the committee supported my stance but am disappointed that the UK Government did not agree to this request.

I have shared my correspondence with the UK Government, in which I raised a number of matters related to the Bill, with both committees and all Members. I hope that this has answered the points raised by the Equality, Human Rights and Social Justice Committee regarding the assurances that I received from the UK Government, and I will be discussing these with the relevant UK Minister when we meet.

I'm committed that the Welsh Government will work with the other Governments of the UK to ensure that the covenant delivers for the armed forces community. This does not mean that every service across the United Kingdom is going to be provided in the same way; it means that every service recognises the needs and circumstances of the armed forces community.

As we move towards implementation, if this Bill is passed, I will ensure that the Welsh Government continues to work closely with our partners and stakeholders in Wales. This includes the armed forces expert group, the Senedd's cross-party group on the armed forces and cadets, our regional armed forces fora and the Welsh Local Government Association's armed forces network. Most important of all, we will continue to engage with the armed forces community and we'll listen to their needs and experiences as they navigate services and support in future.

Bydd elfen cyfamod y Bil hefyd yn ehangu'r ddyletswydd bresennol i 11 maes polisi ychwanegol, gan gynnwys gofal plant, gofal cymdeithasol, trethiant personol a thrafnidiaeth. Ddirprwy Lywydd, mae Bil y Lluoedd Arfog 2026 yn rhoi llwyfan addas i wneud yn siŵr bod gwasanaethau a pholisïau yn ystyried amgylchiadau cymuned y lluoedd arfog yn briodol, a hynny ledled y Deyrnas Gyfunol. Yn yr un modd, mae'n cynnig ffordd o wella tai i deuluoedd y lluoedd arfog a gwella mesurau amddiffyn i ddioddefwyr troseddau'r lluoedd arfog. Mae hefyd yn rhoi mwy o warchodaeth rhag ymddygiad rhywiol a threisgar, stelcio ac aflonyddu ar gyfer y rhai yn y lluoedd arfog, gan gynnwys y rhai sydd wedi'u lleoli yma yng Nghymru.

Dwi'n ddiolchgar i'r Pwyllgor Deddfwriaeth a'r Pwyllgor Cydraddoldeb, Hawliau Dynol a Chyfiawnder Cymdeithasol, ac yn diolch i'r Aelodau am graffu ar y Bil. Dwi'n falch fod y pwyllgor wedi cefnogi fy safbwynt ond yn siomedig na wnaeth Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol gytuno i'r cais hwnnw.

Dwi wedi rhannu fy ngohebiaeth gyda Llywodraeth y Deyrnas Gyfunol, lle codais nifer o faterion yn ymwneud â'r Bil, gyda'r ddau bwyllgor a'r holl Aelodau. Wrth symud i weithredu, os caiff y Bil hwn ei basio, byddaf yn sicrhau bod Llywodraeth Cymru yn parhau i weithio'n agos gyda'n partneriaid a'n rhanddeiliaid yng Nghymru. contributions.item_title_en: 8. Legislative Consent Motion: The Armed Forces Bill
contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr, Ddirprwy Lywydd. In closing this debate, I'd like to thank both the committees and the Members for their contributions to today's debate. I think holding this debate today ensures that the Senedd's views are heard and represented in the passage of this important legislation. That passage is ongoing. The UK Government has today tabled further amendments to the Bill. So, if these amendments are deemed as requiring a further LCM, I will ensure the Senedd are updated and a supplementary LCM is laid.

I want to respond firstly to the points made by the Chair of the Legislation Committee. I absolutely recognise, and I said this in my opening remarks, the importance of providing the Senedd with clear recommendations on legislative consent memoranda at the earliest opportunity to support effective scrutiny. However, I also recognise the importance of laying legislative consent memoranda as soon as possible, rather than delaying them until the Welsh Government has reached a conclusion on its recommendation. I was able to inform the committees of the position once those discussions with the UK Government had taken place. 

As regards the requirement for the new Government to consider this Bill in detail in light of its manifesto commitments, that's why the initial two-week deadline for laying this LCM for the Bill wasn't met. We recognise the difficulties that delayed LCMs cause for effective scrutiny; nonetheless, we are committed to the effective discharge of the legislative consent process and adherence to the two-week deadline.

As regards my recommendation, the Bill makes provision about the armed forces covenant legal duty of due regard, both extending its application to the Welsh Government and extending the policy areas it applies to. We have a programme for government commitment, as I outlined, to uphold the principles of the covenant, and I think this duty will help us and other public bodies to uphold the covenant by requiring the armed forces community to be considered when key decisions on policy are taken.

I want to turn to the points made by the Chair of the human rights, equality and social justice committee—I still want to call it ESJ. On the specific points that you made, I welcome the committee's support for some of the points that I made in my correspondence to the committee. I just want to quickly touch on some of the points that you made, specifically around housing, because I think that the committee raised valid points around the DHS and the disposal of surplus defence land in Wales, which could support our house-building goals. I'm pleased that Welsh Government and MOD officials met on 14 September to discuss this issue and others relating to the DHS. I just want to give assurance that my officials have agreed to work in partnership to explore any opportunities defence land may present in terms of house building and other Government priorities, and I'll update the Senedd as soon as these discussions develop.

I'd also like to make Members aware that, on 30 November, I will be taking a paper to Cabinet regarding our approach to the armed forces covenant to co-ordinate our work across Government and drive progress in the area. We've also convened a Wales covenant conference before that, on 19 November, in Swansea, bringing together the armed forces, UK Government, public bodies and the private and third sectors to share best practice and explore the challenges we need to address collectively around the covenant, many of which have been highlighted by Members across the Siambr today.

I just want to quickly touch on some of the points that you made, specifically around housing, because I think that the committee raised valid points around the DHS and the disposal of surplus defence land in Wales, which could support our house-building goals. I'm pleased that Welsh Government and MOD officials met on 14 September to discuss this issue and others relating to the DHS. I just want to give assurance that my officials have agreed to work in partnership to explore any opportunities defence land may present in terms of house building and other Government priorities, and I'll update the Senedd as soon as these discussions develop.

I'd also like to make Members aware that, on 30 November, I will be taking a paper to Cabinet regarding our approach to the armed forces covenant to co-ordinate our work across Government and drive progress in the area. We've also convened a Wales covenant conference before that, on 19 November, in Swansea, bringing together the armed forces, UK Government, public bodies and the private and third sectors to share best practice and explore the challenges we need to address collectively around the covenant, many of which have been highlighted by Members across the Siambr today.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Legislative Consent Motion: The Armed Forces Bill
contributions.text_english: To conclude, I believe that support for the armed forces community should unite us all in this Chamber. To recognise the positive effects of this Bill, I recommend that the Senedd supports the Bill and gives its consent. Thank you.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr. I do recognise the specific way that poverty and deprivation can affect rural areas in particular. So, one of the things that I did was make sure that, when I announced funding for local authorities that provides support for wider poverty prevention activities and also emergency food aid, which include those community hubs where preventative services are provided, that funding also included an allocation for rural local authorities, a rural allocation, recognising the added challenges of delivering support in rural areas. That rural premium element has been included on a test-and-learn basis, to recognise the additional challenges, as the Member has outlined, and also the costs that rural local authorities and other services can face when delivering cost-of-living and poverty support.

On your broader question, obviously, a fair and prosperous Wales, the whole of Wales, is the long-term vision of this Government, and it's reasserted in our programme for government. A key part of this vision is to support rural areas by policies across Government designed to bring tangible benefits to our rural communities. Our rural communities are diverse, they have diverse needs, they face challenges due to geography and distance and cost and scalability. And we know about ageing population in rural areas, lack of employment opportunities, lower wages and, of course, infrequent transport provisions. So, we're bringing forward a legislative duty on rural-proofing, and that's expected to bring long-term benefits to rural communities, considering their specific circumstances, and, of course, that is something that will apply across all Government policies.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english: Thank you very much for that supplementary question, specifically about Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd, which is a constituency, of course, that I share. But, as I said, we as a Government are determined that the support that we can provide does reach those who are most in need, including those households that are facing additional challenges and additional costs related to being part of a rural area, as I set out in my earlier answer. We believe that local authorities have the best understanding and information on how to support those communities. So, we have given those local authorities guidelines to go with the funding that the Member referred to, to ensure that that funding does go to those who need it most, but also that they have some discretion to use that funding for the projects and schemes that would have the biggest impact. We will work closely now with our partners to ensure that we look at how that funding is having an effect, who it reaches, and how effective it will be, as I said, with this test-and-learn system, to ensure that that funding is being used effectively.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, and I recognise as well the campaigning that the Member has done on the availability and cost of childcare and the effect of that not only on families in poverty, but also in terms of gender inequality that affects women mostly.

You mentioned the analysis made by the Bevan Foundation in terms of the new model that should, or the best model that could, provide childcare to all in a way that is fair and reaches the aim. I agree with that—that there are challenges and important decisions that need to be made—but also, as the Bevan Foundation has underlined, that there is an opportunity now to do things differently and better. I agree that the system currently is too complex and too costly, and that's at the heart of our programme for developing and expanding and making sure that the system we have evolves for the better.

So, I think, in terms of the timetable, you'll know that we have spoken about taking a step-by-step approach that's essential to ensure that we do this in a sustainable manner and that takes into consideration the needs of providers and parents. We will be able to say by the end of this financial year—so, in less than a year of this Government's time—that every two-year-old child can be offered childcare wherever they live of 12.5 hours, and I will update the Senedd later on this term, probably at the beginning of December, as to what the next steps will be.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english: I think there's a fundamental misunderstanding here. The Equality and Human Rights Commission's code of practice for services, public functions and associations, which came into force on 5 August, means that we have to comply with our legal duties as a Government in respect of the Equality Act 2010. All bodies and service providers must themselves ensure that they're complying with the law. The Welsh Government of course expects all organisations to comply with the law, and we've clearly stated that. But the application then means careful consideration of the guidance in each situation. It is the responsibility of all the bodies and service providers to do that. The EHRC is the regulator to ensure that that is happening. They are responsible for monitoring compliance with equality and human rights law, ensuring that public authorities and other duty bearers meet their obligations. That isn't a responsibility of the Government.

The figures will become clear in the forthcoming draft budget. You will be able to scrutinise that, the committees will be able to scrutinise that, and, of course, questions can be asked here of Ministers around their spending plans. 

You're asking about progress. In terms of the money that we've already spent, you'll know that there was £55 million in total allocated in the supplementary budget, which we have put to work in terms of expanding childcare and also with some capital grants to enable that to happen. So, 78.9 per cent of all two-year-olds are now offered childcare. Over 13,000 new two-year-olds have been offered a childcare place. Over 9,900 new two-year-olds attended their funded childcare, and over 2,000 of those children attended funded childcare in a Welsh-medium setting. 

As I said, we are now expecting, and I've had assurances from local authorities—. Many Members in the Chamber will probably see this happening now—their local authorities putting out that offer to parents of that age group. That's happening progressively in the way that we said it would. And then, by the end of the financial year, all two-year-olds in Wales, in every single local authority, will be offered 12.5 hours of funded childcare. I think there are quite a lot of statistics there for you.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english:
We are of course, as I'll reiterate again, absolutely committed to upholding the principles of the armed forces covenant, ensuring fair access to healthcare, housing, employment, education, skills and training for veterans and their families. The covenant is absolutely a social justice issue, reducing the potential for disadvantage from serving in the armed forces. By and large, service in the armed forces does lead to positive outcomes. I have submitted a legislative consent memorandum to the Senedd in respect of the Armed Forces Bill, including its plans for broadening the armed forces covenant.

The covenant, of course, doesn't specify outcomes or targets. It's about consideration. It's about understanding why there needs to be a specific way of working, to be adapted insofar as the services that veterans may come in contact with, to reduce that disadvantage and to afford a special consideration. It's clear that plans for broadening the armed forces covenant will impact the way we work, and so we need to consider policy now across a broad range of areas through that armed forces lens. We already have the ways and means to do that in other areas, of course, through our integrated impact assessment process.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english:
I just want to reflect first of all that there seems to be the suggestion that there's some kind of malign motivation behind the fact that we want to evolve this model, and there absolutely isn't. Local authorities, of course, have been engaged with us from the very beginning. There’s a WLGA representative on the expert group, and has been from the early days of this Government, because we started work on this commitment, as you would expect, immediately after the Cabinet was formed. They have always been fully in the loop.

As regards the moving away from that model, that's absolutely not what this is about. It's about evolving what it is. The main reason why we want to call something Welsh Government-funded childcare is for the very reason, as I outlined earlier, that people, now we’re making a universal offer, don't think they're eligible, because they're so used to the Flying Start geographical cliff edge that means that somebody in one street is eligible and somebody on the other street isn't. So, what we wanted to do in the promotion of our rolling out of universal childcare is make that clear. That was the sole motivation: it was a communication to make it clear to parents that they were now eligible for that universal offer.

contributions.text_english: That is absolutely our intention. You will know, as the former Chair—. I think you conducted an inquiry when you were Chair of the Children, Young People and Education Committee in the Senedd before last. I think you did an inquiry on outreach and on how that approach wasn't reaching all those in need. So, I know that you understand this well. contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english: Diolch. The Member is absolutely right as regards economic prosperity. Making sure that we have well-paid jobs and jobs that pay fairly and have fair work conditions is absolutely key to making sure that we can lift families out of poverty. But I do reject the narrative around dependency on benefits. People are eligible for those benefits because their income is currently not sufficient to make sure that they are able to live with dignity and meet their essential needs. I think there is a fundamental difference of values and principles between us on this. We will absolutely make sure that every penny that this Government spends—and, obviously, the Member knows that welfare policy is not devolved to Wales—goes to those who most need that support. And of course, we will not be quibbling about who is eligible for that support. If they are in need, if they are in poverty, if they are disabled and need our help, then we will help them.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english:
Well, I'm glad that you agree with me and I hope you were listening carefully to the action we are taking on affordable childcare. That's why it's one of our main priorities as a Government and one of the main policies that, of course, I'm working on. It's a transformational, complex policy, but we absolutely know that it is fundamental to making sure that we can make those costs less for families and also give them the opportunity to be able to get back into the labour market and also increase their hours and get back into training and education.

On the point on how we're doing things differently, well, I have already said and set out, and reiterated this in my scrutiny session in committee last week, that I am not going to be throwing the baby out with the bath water as regards the child poverty strategy. But I do think that it needs a tighter focus and I do think that it needs measurable targets and milestones for us to make sure that what we are doing is having the desired effect and the intended effect.

So, I have already started work on developing and focusing in on what that more honed child poverty strategy can look like, and, as I said, including thinking about how we can evaluate as we go along, making sure we measure our progress. So, we will be working on that, we're developing it with stakeholders, considering, then, how to report on that progress to show what impact we are having. And I've already met with our external reference group and I've also met across Cabinet as well. We've got a cross-Cabinet taskforce on this very issue to make sure that we are aligned on our ambitions for that strategy and the types of targets we think will be useful to guide our work.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice
contributions.text_english: We are committed to ensuring that childcare expansion works for families in all parts of Wales, and that's including rural communities, where provision can be more dispersed and can be more fragile. So, we already have some flexibility in the system through guidance, through funding and local authority planning. But we are, as a part of this expansion programme, actively looking at what more can be done to ensure childcare hours and transport solutions and capital investment all respond to the specific needs of rural communities. So, local authorities use childcare sufficiency assessments and annual action plans to identify those gaps in provision, including those rural challenges, and we continue to support practical solutions, then, such as co-locations with schools and community hubs. We also recognise that childminders are really important as well in rural communities, and so we're working with partners, including Cwlwm, to support workforce development, business sustainability and provider capacity.

contributions.text_english:
I fully recognise those concerns. I'm sure that they are familiar to us all. Those services are crucial to our communities, particularly for people who perhaps can't use public transport or there is no transport available to take them to the next town. They are an important part of our town centres and high streets, and that is the Government's view, most certainly.

But, again, issues related to post offices are not devolved to Welsh Ministers. As I mentioned in an earlier response, the UK Government's commitment to post offices includes plans to retain the size of the network as it is, and that means looking for new businesses to offer those services when individual post offices close. But it also includes a commitment to locate post offices in town centres, where possible. Because, as I said, I agree—we know that post offices increase the number of visitors to the high street, as well as providing those crucial services.

Our programme for government does include a commitment to look at those options to rejuvenate our town centres, and that links to our work in terms of the town-centre taskforce that we've established. contributions.text_english:
I'd like to clarify the reason why it says 'seek to pilot': it's because there's a very important decision that needs to be made by the UK Treasury, because what we don't want to do with Cynnal is make families worse off. We want to make them better off. So, that means the UK Treasury has to give a benefit and tax disregard. We heard some encouraging signs in an interview with Andy Burnham during the Labour conference on that. It's something, of course, that I've been pressing on with the UK Treasury, and so of course has the Cabinet Minister for Finance, because we want them to allow us to—. We have the powers to pilot the payment, but what we don't have are the powers over that tax and benefit disregard. So, that's why we are saying 'seek to pilot', because we don't have—. We wouldn't want to do something if we didn't have that assurance from UK Treasury that it wouldn't make families worse off. 

We are preparing to implement that pilot. We've commissioned an expert team to help lead on that design, thinking about then, obviously, again, the monitoring and evaluation. We want it to be effective. We've already met four times, and we're meeting again in a few weeks' time. It's been an intense piece of work. It's an intense process because we do want to make sure that we can get this payment out to families—a payment that has proven so successful in Scotland in lowering rates of child poverty—out to children who are in need as soon as we possibly can.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. I'm very pleased to provide this update today on the work to develop the initial phasing and costs of the Government's ambitious commitment to deliver a universal childcare offer.

Members will be aware that the Government is introducing a phased expansion of funded universal childcare, which, at full roll-out, will be the most generous offer in the UK, providing 20 hours of funded childcare each week, for 48 weeks of the year, for all children aged from nine months to four years old.

In my view, and the view of the Government, and in the view of every expert on poverty and child development, the expansion of childcare is not merely a 'nice to have', but it's absolutely essential. Whether or not to expand funded childcare is not a question to discuss. The lack of affordable childcare is a societal problem to solve, and in solving it, we will deliver benefits that span across gender equality, early child development, tackling poverty, supporting our economy, and improving our children's health and educational outcomes.

Having stated with pride our aim of delivering a universal childcare offer, and with us now 57 days into this Government term, we have progressed with this and made excellent progress. We have been working on our plans with local government and sector representatives through the newly established expert group, and we have already announced an additional £55 million of funding through the supplementary budget to support the initial phase of the expansion programme.

As part of the process of developing our manifesto, we carefully costed an expanded childcare offer, and we identified the additional funding required to deliver the full expansion. And now in Government, officials have undertaken further economic modelling.

On that basis, we are developing clearer costs, considering the assumptions behind them. The modelling undertaken so far suggests that, at today's prices, the core costs of the full expansion of our offer will require an additional £375 million a year. This is a mid-point estimate, and work is ongoing with our economists and analysts to test and model a range of variables, which includes the costs at each phase of expansion and potential take-up rates.

As advised by our expansion of childcare expert steering group, we will also take into account not only workforce costs, but a range of factors, including training and development, additional learning needs, local authority support and capital. The level of additional funding required, indicated by Welsh Government economists to date, aligns with the detailed work undertaken by Plaid Cymru in preparation to make this policy commitment.

Our clear aim is that families of all children from nine months to four years across Wales should be able to access a more affordable, simpler, more consistent childcare offer by the end of this Senedd term. Achieving this aim will require careful sequencing, along with partnership working and ongoing funding decisions, but we are determined to maintain the momentum.

The latest data, published on 1 July, shows that we are now offering funded childcare to nearly 75 per cent of all two-year-olds across Wales in 2025-26. However, we want to go further and ensure that what was promised by the previous Labour Government, but not delivered, is fully implemented. I want us to reach all our two-year-old children as quickly as possible and I am urging local authorities to complete this first phase by the end of this financial year. This is what families want and deserve.

At the start of this Government term, three local authorities had succeeded in completing the roll-out of 12.5 hours of funded childcare to all two-year olds. One other local authority has reached every two-year-old child last month. And 16 more local authorities have already confirmed that, with the additional funding that we will invest through the supplementary budget, they'll be able to move to a full roll-out by the end of this financial year, which demonstrates our commitment to deliver our new offer to families across Wales. Officials are working closely with the remaining two local authorities to understand how they can be supported to deliver this phase at this point.

Diolch yn fawr, Lywydd. Dwi'n falch iawn o roi'r diweddariad yma heddiw ar y gwaith i ddatblygu camau a chostau cychwynnol ymrwymiad uchelgeisiol y Llywodraeth yma i ddarparu cynnig gofal plant i bob teulu.

Bydd yr Aelodau yn ymwybodol bod y Llywodraeth wrthi'n cyflwyno proses raddol i ehangu cynnig gofal plant i bob teulu sydd wedi'i ariannu, ac, o'i weithredu'n llawn, mai hwn fydd y cynnig mwyaf hael yn y Deyrnas Gyfunol, gan ddarparu 20 awr o ofal wedi'i ariannu bob wythnos, am 48 wythnos o'r flwyddyn, i bob plentyn rhwng naw mis a phedair oed.

Yn fy marn i, ac ym marn y Llywodraeth, ac ym marn pob arbenigwr ar dlodi a datblygiad plant, nid rhywbeth y byddai'n braf ei gael yw darpariaeth gofal plant ehangach, ond mae'n gwbl hanfodol. Dyw 'A ddylen ni fod yn ehangu gofal plant wedi'i ariannu neu beidio?' ddim yn gwestiwn i'w drafod. Mae'r diffyg gofal plant fforddiadwy yn broblem gymdeithasol i'w datrys, ac o'i datrys, fe fyddwn ni'n creu manteision sy'n ymestyn i gydraddoldeb rhywedd, datblygiad cynnar plant, mynd i'r afael â thlodi, cefnogi ein heconomi, a gwella iechyd a chyrhaeddiad addysg ein plant.

Ar ôl datgan gyda balchder ein nod i ddarparu cynnig gofal plant i bob teulu, a ninnau nawr 57 o ddiwrnodau i mewn i dymor y Llywodraeth hon, rŷn ni wedi bwrw iddi ac yn gwneud cynnydd rhagorol. Rŷn ni wedi bod yn cydweithio ar ein cynlluniau gyda chynrychiolwyr y sector a llywodraeth leol drwy'r grŵp arbenigol sydd wedi ei sefydlu gennym ni, ac rŷn ni eisoes wedi cyhoeddi cyllid o £55 miliwn ychwanegol drwy'r gyllideb atodol tuag at gam cychwynnol y rhaglen ehangu. 

Fel rhan o'r broses o ddatblygu ein maniffesto, fe wnaethon ni gyfrifo'n ofalus gostau ehangu'r cynnig gofal plant, a nodi'r cyllid ychwanegol yr oedd ei angen er mwyn mynd ati i'w ehangu'n llawn. A ninnau nawr yn Llywodraeth, mae swyddogion wedi creu modelau economaidd pellach.

Ar y sail honno, rŷn ni'n datblygu costau cliriach gan ystyried y rhagdybiaethau sydd y tu ôl iddyn nhw. Mae'r modelau sydd wedi'u creu hyd yma yn awgrymu y bydd costau craidd ehangu ein cynnig yn llawn, ar sail prisiau heddiw, yn galw am £375 miliwn yn ychwanegol y flwyddyn. Amcangyfrif canolig yw hyn, ac mae gwaith ar y gweill gyda'n heconomegwyr a'n dadansoddwyr i brofi a modelu cyfres o elfennau newidiol, sy'n cynnwys y costau ar bob cam ehangu a'r niferoedd posibl a fydd yn manteisio ar y cynnig.

Yn unol â chyngor ein grŵp llywio arbenigol ar ehangu gofal plant, fe fyddwn ni'n ystyried nid dim ond costau'r gweithlu, ond ystod o ffactorau, gan gynnwys hyfforddiant a datblygiad, anghenion dysgu ychwanegol, cymorth awdurdodau lleol a chyfalaf. Mae lefel y cyllid ychwanegol sydd ei angen, a nodwyd gan waith economegwyr Llywodraeth Cymru hyd yma, yn gyson â gwaith manwl Plaid Cymru wrth baratoi i wneud yr ymrwymiad polisi hwn.

Ein nod clir yw bod teuluoedd yn gallu cael mynediad at ofal plant mwy fforddiadwy a symlach, mwy cyson i bob plentyn rhwng naw mis a phedair oed ledled Cymru erbyn diwedd y tymor seneddol hwn. Bydd angen gofal wrth osod trefn ar y camau i'w dilyn i gyrraedd y nod, ynghyd â gwaith partneriaeth a phenderfyniadau cyllido wrth symud ymlaen, ond rŷn ni'n benderfynol o gynnal y momentwm.

Mae'r data diweddaraf, a gyhoeddwyd ar 1 Gorffennaf, yn dangos ein bod ni bellach yn cynnig gofal plant wedi ei ariannu i bron 75 y cant o blant dwy oed ledled Cymru yn 2025-26. Fodd bynnag, rŷn ni am fynd ymhellach a sicrhau bod yr hyn a addawyd gan y Llywodraeth Lafur ddiwethaf, ond na chyflawnwyd ganddi, yn cael ei weithredu'n llawn. Dwi eisiau inni gyrraedd ein holl blant dwy oed cyn gynted â phosibl, a dwi'n pwyso ar awdurdodau lleol i gwblhau'r cam cyntaf hwn erbyn diwedd y flwyddyn ariannol. Dyma beth mae teuluoedd eisiau ei weld ac yn ei haeddu.

Ar ddechrau tymor y Llywodraeth hon, roedd tri awdurdod lleol wedi llwyddo i gynnig 12.5 awr o ofal wedi'i ariannu i bob plentyn dwy oed. Mae un awdurdod lleol arall wedi cyrraedd pob plentyn dwyflwydd oed y mis diwethaf. Ac mae 16 awdurdod lleol arall eisoes wedi cadarnhau, yn sgil y cyllid ychwanegol y byddwn yn ei fuddsoddi drwy'r gyllideb atodol, y byddan nhw'n gallu cyflwyno'r ddarpariaeth yn llawn erbyn diwedd y flwyddyn ariannol hon, sy'n arddangos ein hymrwymiad i ddarparu ein cynnig newydd i deuluoedd ledled Cymru. Mae swyddogion yn gweithio'n agos gyda'r ddau awdurdod lleol sy'n weddill er mwyn deall sut i'w cefnogi i ddarparu i'r pwynt hwn.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
Partnership working is a key element of delivery, and I met local authorities and Cwlwm earlier today as part of a workshop to discuss the practical challenges and opportunities of delivery and how to work together to deliver accessible childcare to more families at pace.

The childcare landscape in Wales is unnecessarily complex—for providers, partners and parents—and we are building on existing programmes, entitlements and delivery arrangements, while looking honestly at complexity, barriers and unnecessary burdens. I am determined to maintain momentum and enable local authorities and providers to move as quickly as possible through the phases of delivery.

So, after rolling out 12.5 hours for all two-year-olds, the focus will be on increasing provision for two-year-olds to 20 hours and 48 weeks. We will consider flexibility on the pace of the roll-out, based on local circumstances, encouraging expansion to go further and faster where possible, so that families are supported quickly. Some areas and providers will be able to increase hours, weeks or both more quickly than others, however, I am encouraging and expecting a laser focus on delivering this commitment. 

In areas that have already rolled out 12.5 hours, they will be encouraged to take the next step of expansion, offering additional hours and weeks of the year, depending on practicalities locally. And, in parallel, I want local authorities to start working with all providers to roll out the expanded offer to three and four-year-olds on a universal basis, and will be working with officials later this year to plan the resources and funding that this will require.

This element will build on nursery education and will ensure that all children in this cohort, not just those whose parents meet the current eligibility criteria, will be able to access the benefits and enrichment of quality childcare. We will sequence this carefully, building on our existing offers for two-year-olds and three and four-year-olds, before moving to the final phase: 20 hours of universal childcare for children aged nine months to two years.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
The childcare workforce is central to expansion, which depends on the capacity, skills and support needed to deliver high-quality provision. Our economists and analysts are developing projections of how many staff we will need and where we will need them as we work through the delivery of these next phases. In partnership with the sector, we are exploring ideas and developing options to support workforce growth. We will produce a workforce plan that will outline how we will support the growth, recruitment and retention of the childcare workforce, improving working conditions and career pathways.

I fully expect that Members and colleagues—and, most importantly, parents and carers—will continue to monitor our further announcements as we deliver on this commitment. But it is a pleasure to be here to not just discuss but begin to deliver universal funded childcare. We are moving the dial for children and families after years of treating childcare support as an optional add-on. We know that this will require significant investment. We know that this is an ambitious, complex commitment, but it is absolutely the right thing to do. Wales has the highest childcare costs in the UK, with many households spending more than their rent or mortgage on childcare costs. Women are disproportionately affected by this, and Wales has a persistent gender pay gap. Wales has some of the poorest children who cannot currently access the benefits of early years provision. We are making our commitment to change this a reality by delivering a childcare system that works for children and families. Diolch yn fawr.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
It does baffle me, you know. You said that this was very much welcomed on the doorstep. Well, we've seen the result of that, haven't we? We know that for years and years anti-poverty researchers and people who are trying to promote equality in Wales and in our society have seen this as a keystone, a foundational part of addressing that inequality. And yet all we get from Reform is talk about a worst-case scenario, a financial liability. And, of course, you didn't even mention it in your manifesto, because you had not realised, actually—. Or perhaps you're just not interested in reducing inequality. But this Government is, and this Government is delivering. 

You asked me about delivery. I have just outlined to you the first phase and the initial costing of that. I have told you that by the end of this financial year, working with our partners in local authorities and providers, every child that is two years old in Wales will be entitled to 12.5 hours of childcare. That's the first phase. We have delivered at pace on that. We are delivering at pace on that. When we came into this Government, three local authorities had managed to achieve that after many years of this being a Welsh Government policy under the last administration.

So, I'm not going to take the criticism that we are not delivering. We absolutely are. Fifty-seven days into this Government, we absolutely are delivering on this first phase. I've been extremely clear from the beginning. Perhaps you weren't listening to the debate. Perhaps you would have done better in the election if you had. But our party made it absolutely clear that this was a phased plan. Anyone who knows anything about childcare is going to understand the complexity of the current system. I suggest you do a little bit of reading in order to see what the complex landscape is at the moment. That's why we have an expert group steering us in this work.

I have also mentioned the midpoint. As I set out in my statement, there are variables here. There are variables as regards the modelling, and that's the work we're doing. The figure that I set out is the midpoint of the take-up that we have seen in other parts of the UK that have similar demographics, which we could then reasonably expect would be reflected here in Wales. But, of course, we know that the full cost of this modelling—. The maximum is usually about 80 per cent take-up. The additional funding that would be needed would be between £250 million and £500 million. The £375 million is a midpoint estimate. The precise funding will always depend on take-up rates. We have to have estimates and modelling around all those scenarios. That's why the work is ongoing. It's not about making a plan, it's about making sure that we can deliver what is actually needed as we work through these phases. We will always be able to respond then to any emerging trends that we see happen. This is an ambitious policy. We would hope that, if we build it, they will come.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr for the questions. As regards Flying Start, as I've said, this isn't about—and I've said in previous statements, and I hope I've outlined it here again today—just adding hours; absolutely not. This is about taking a system-wide approach to transforming support for children in the early years. Childcare, as I said, is our manifesto commitment. It's absolutely a key part of that, and so, of course, the immediate priority is to make sure that we can start that work of rolling out what we've promised to the Welsh electorate, and then build, as I say, towards the next stages of expansion, as I've mapped out today.

But the wider support services that are associated with early intervention and prevention programmes, such as Flying Start and Families First, of course, with that enhanced health visiting, with the parental support and speech, language and communication support, of course—they're absolutely fundamental to the preventative agenda of this Government. I absolutely recognise that they are vital for supporting children and families who need that additional help in the work that we want to do to reduce inequalities for disadvantaged children specifically. So, the expansion itself is focused on funded childcare, but as an absolute part of that work, we want to move towards a clearer, more consistent and more unified system across the piece, protecting the wider support that children have that helps them get the best start in life. So, that approach will evolve over time.

As regards the workforce, you're absolutely right as regards the workforce. We know that we've got a lot of work to do here. That's why we're going to bring forward a specific plan. That will be in the autumn, because I think it will be aligned with what we're going to need to have conversations with the Cabinet Minister for Finance about. But our expert steering group absolutely has workforce planning at the top of its agenda, and we are listening to partners in the sector around what we can do, the creative solutions we can have and the incentivisation around recruitment and retention that we can bring forward there. So, as I say, it's absolutely central. We have to have the capacity, the skills and the support in place to deliver the provision that we want for our children. We're currently working on estimates, as I said, based on the modelling that we're doing. We'll turn that into a workforce plan, building on existing provision with our partners, with Social Care Wales, with local authorities and Cwlwm to have that sharp focus. As I said, it will build on existing provision, but we know we need to go further.

You also asked me about the role of the expert steering group. The economist that you mentioned is one of the lead economists in the UK that looks at early years and childcare provision throughout the UK. He's published papers on what's happened, for instance, in England. That group, I think, very well represents the voices we need in the room, but it isn't limited, and that's in the terms of reference of the steering group. We do bring in independent experts and have presentations from them. We had somebody from the Department for Education last week, someone who was key in designing the roll-out in England, for us to be able to hear from him and also to hear about the lessons that need to be learned, because we don't want to replicate any of the unintended consequences that we've seen in some regards in what's happened with the roll-out in England. So, those unintended consequences or worsening inequalities are absolutely not what we want to have, and so we are thoroughly considering that. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
In the first point, really, you were querying about the midpoint, and I think I've tried to explain. I think we said in our manifesto it was going to be around £400 million additional, so what we're seeing as the midpoint—that was modelled on a midpoint as well. It’s the common practice. So, the midpoint that we've modelled here is £375 million. But as I said, obviously—because this is demand-led, this is a new thing—we're hoping that all the discussion around childcare will make sure—. And the point you made around simplifying the process too—we know that many people don't take up childcare, not only because it's disjointed, but because it's difficult, it's complex and there are so many different eligibility thresholds, things you've got to apply for at different points during your child's life. So, I can assure you that the point around simplification and what that looks like, what that front door looks like, is absolutely part of this work as well. And my officials are already working on that. So, it isn't higher, actually; it's around the same as what we projected, but we do recognise, of course, that there are all kinds of variables as we push forward towards the next phases that we need to allow for. But I do welcome your support for this initiative, for this policy, and, as I said, I agree absolutely on your point around simplifying the system.

On your point around the way this policy interacts with other policy areas, it does, obviously, around education. Part of this work is about—. We've seen, haven't we, it's been exacerbated since COVID, but we've seen for a long time that families do need more support in order to make sure that their children are ready to learn, and this is going to play a big part in that. So, I'm having conversations—I actually met yesterday again with the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language. We are working on how we can measure that, how we can evaluate the effect that this will have on that readiness to learn while keeping that absolutely child-centred, that evaluation. So, it will interact across Government and, as I said, especially with health, the interventions, the team around the family, and that support we will absolutely retain, but in a different form as we roll out this universal system.

You asked me about exactly how the additional funding from the supplementary budget was going to be utilised. We've said that we're going to invest an additional £55 million in the additional budget. So, hopefully, if you support this policy, you can support that budget this afternoon. Twenty million pounds of that will help to accelerate the roll-out, so that's the work we've indicated to local authorities that they're able to utilise in order to make sure that we get to the point where funded childcare is available to all two-year-olds in Wales by the end of this financial year. Then there's £10 million of capital funding, which is going to help enhance and expand childcare settings, improving quality and capacity and accessibility of early years provision. And then £25 million of that is going to be used to support the wider system, including managing rising demand, because we're talking about it a lot more now—it's been such a front-and-centre policy during the election. People are coming to access more provision, which is great. We need to make it easier for them and more affordable for them. We want to strengthen the long-term sustainability of providers, and that's something you talked about as well. And that is something that is absolutely crucial as well, and, again, is part of the work that we're doing. So, we're already investing in that, and, of course, supporting Welsh-medium childcare is part of that as well.

So, on the last point on safeguarding, I think it is a really important point, and quality, you know, with the national minimum standard, which was updated last month. Wales has the highest national standards issued under the Children and Families (Wales) Measure 2010, and the Child Minding and Day Care (Wales) Regulations 2010, and Care Inspectorate Wales, of course is a regulatory body, so we will always make sure that anyone who is registered for providing day care and child minding will be inspected according to those regulations.

We are looking at creative solutions. You know, I think we really need to consider child minders in this, who are constantly coming up as 'excellent' and 'good' when they're inspected. They provide such a valuable service for people who work irregular hours, especially in places where there isn't a density of population. So, we will absolutely be considering other models of provision as we roll this out.
contributions.text_original:
In the first point, really, you were querying about the midpoint, and I think I've tried to explain. I think we said in our manifesto it was going to be around £400 million additional, so what we're seeing as the midpoint—that was modelled on a midpoint as well. It’s the common practice. So, the midpoint that we've modelled here is £375 million. But as I said, obviously—because this is demand-led, this is a new thing—we're hoping that all the discussion around childcare will make sure—. And the point you made around simplifying the process too—we know that many people don't take up childcare, not only because it's disjointed, but because it's difficult, it's complex and there are so many different eligibility thresholds, things you've got to apply for at different points during your child's life. So, I can assure you that the point around simplification and what that looks like, what that front door looks like, is absolutely part of this work as well. And my officials are already working on that. So, it isn't higher, actually; it's around the same as what we projected, but we do recognise, of course, that there are all kinds of variables as we push forward towards the next phases that we need to allow for. But I do welcome your support for this initiative, for this policy, and, as I said, I agree absolutely on your point around simplifying the system.

On your point around the way this policy interacts with other policy areas, it does, obviously, around education. Part of this work is about—. We've seen, haven't we, it's been exacerbated since COVID, but we've seen for a long time that families do need more support in order to make sure that their children are ready to learn, and this is going to play a big part in that. So, I'm having conversations—I actually met yesterday again with the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language. We are working on how we can measure that, how we can evaluate the effect that this will have on that readiness to learn while keeping that absolutely child-centred, that evaluation. So, it will interact across Government and, as I said, especially with health, the interventions, the team around the family, and that support we will absolutely retain, but in a different form as we roll out this universal system.

You asked me about exactly how the additional funding from the supplementary budget was going to be utilised. We've said that we're going to invest an additional £55 million in the additional budget. So, hopefully, if you support this policy, you can support that budget this afternoon. Twenty million pounds of that will help to accelerate the roll-out, so that's the work we've indicated to local authorities that they're able to utilise in order to make sure that we get to the point where funded childcare is available to all two-year-olds in Wales by the end of this financial year. Then there's £10 million of capital funding, which is going to help enhance and expand childcare settings, improving quality and capacity and accessibility of early years provision. And then £25 million of that is going to be used to support the wider system, including managing rising demand, because we're talking about it a lot more now—it's been such a front-and-centre policy during the election. People are coming to access more provision, which is great. We need to make it easier for them and more affordable for them. We want to strengthen the long-term sustainability of providers, and that's something you talked about as well. And that is something that is absolutely crucial as well, and, again, is part of the work that we're doing. So, we're already investing in that, and, of course, supporting Welsh-medium childcare is part of that as well.

So, on the last point on safeguarding, I think it is a really important point, and quality, you know, with the national minimum standard, which was updated last month. Wales has the highest national standards issued under the Children and Families (Wales) Measure 2010, and the Child Minding and Day Care (Wales) Regulations 2010, and Care Inspectorate Wales, of course is a regulatory body, so we will always make sure that anyone who is registered for providing day care and child minding will be inspected according to those regulations.

We are looking at creative solutions. You know, I think we really need to consider child minders in this, who are constantly coming up as 'excellent' and 'good' when they're inspected. They provide such a valuable service for people who work irregular hours, especially in places where there isn't a density of population. So, we will absolutely be considering other models of provision as we roll this out.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
Diolch yn fawr. I really do welcome the support. I'm really excited about this policy, and we saw that excitement on the doors, didn't we? Because I think you can compare it. When we deliver this, it will be up there with the most—well, the most—generous offer in the UK, certainly—world leading, actually. There are nations that are very much ahead of us, but I think that this is something that should be a real badge of honour for Wales. More than that, it won't be an empty badge of honour; this will be something that makes a real difference to people's lives. So, I think it's great to see the enthusiasm for this expansion. I'm hearing it from stakeholders and partners.

It is a significant commitment, and, yes, it will require a substantial increase in workforce numbers. So, as I said, this is a key theme of the work of our expert group. We are developing those projections of how many staff we're going to need, where we're going to need them as we're working through these phases. A specific phase of that expansion is to extend the funded childcare to nine months to two years. We know that will require a step change in provision. This is completely new. The first two phases are building on something that is already provided in part. This will be new, so there will be specific actions needed there to grow the workforce. That'll be informed by the work we're currently doing. I'll update colleagues regularly as we reach that phase.

Of course, Welsh-medium provision, as you would expect, is a core element of this expansion and a core concern of this Government. So, we're working closely with Mudiad Meithrin. The chief executive, Dr Catrin Edwards, is a member of the expert steering group. We are already taking measures now. We announced a new pilot scheme, which is coming through the National Centre for Learning Welsh, to build the Welsh language skills of our childcare workforce in order to increase that capacity.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english: This statement is specifically on the childcare expansion, but I accept, of course, that these things are linked. Play is within my portfolio; I'm not speaking about that today, but I would encourage you to ask me questions about that when I am here to answer questions on my broader portfolio. But I would say that ensuring children have access to childcare absolutely helps to socialise them, to bring out that play, which we know is absolutely key to children's development. As I said before, this is about making children also more ready for school and learning, getting into that foundation phase. But I would encourage you to perhaps ask me a question or write to me specifically about your concerns as regards play.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
I absolutely agree that childcare costs across Wales are prohibitively high. One of the reasons for this policy is understanding that it will be a mitigation against the high cost of living for families. It will put money back in people's pockets, and parents, especially mothers, of course, can find themselves locked out of the labour market, and children then, of course, prevented from accessing all the benefits of quality childcare. So, as regards prioritisation, we're committed to make progress on the expansion as soon as we can. As I mentioned in my statement, we're making very good progress to offer childcare to all two-year-olds all over Wales, and we're urging all local authorities to work with us to complete this stage, and, as I say, the vast majority of them are there and will be there.

So, at the moment, thousands of children across Wales don't get any childcare support, and so we're going to go from that current reality to a system where all families are able to access support, but we have to add to that support incrementally until we reach our full commitment. But by proceeding with and getting early momentum with this initial phase, I think, of getting 12.5 hours funded childcare to all two-year-olds, we're really laying the foundations of that truly universal funded childcare offer, which, as I say, is something only a handful of countries in the world have achieved.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
Thank you for the question. I think I just answered the question in that we absolutely recognise the need for better benchmarking; we simply haven't got that in place. It exists in parts, but it isn't satisfactory and isn't measuring what we think we need it to measure.

Having seen learning from childcare provision both in the UK and internationally, we can see that, for instance, 100 per cent is unlikely. However, as work continues on developing this policy, we are, as I said, going to respond to any emerging trend, and that will include demand. And we remain ready and willing—and that's why this work has to be planned and phased in this way, in order to respond to those things—to adjust and refine our plans. But this is an ambitious Government, as I said, and we fully hope that as many children as possible take up the offer that we'll be able to give them.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much to the Member for the question, and thank you very much for the support and for the campaigning work that you and others in this Chamber have done on this crucial policy area. I'm pleased that you share our ambition for the children of Wales, and I know you do. 

In terms of that voice on the panel, Cwlwm, as you mentioned, are represented on the panel, but also there is a representative from the WLGA, who of course represents all of Wales's local authorities. So, they are vocal and taking those messages from their councils in terms of the particular situation in the many diverse areas of Wales. And as I mentioned, this group is not limited.
